Examples

Examples - Physical Quantities

Solved Examples

Example 1: Significant Figures

Question: Find the number of significant figures in 0.0025. Solution: Leading zeros are not significant. Only digits 2 and 5 are significant. Answer: 2 significant figures.

Example 2: Unit Conversion

Question: Convert 1 J to ergs. Solution: 1 J = 1 kg m^2/s^2. In CGS: 1 kg = 10^3 g, 1 m = 10^2 cm. 1 J = 10^3 x (10^2)^2 = 10^3 x 10^4 g cm^2/s^2 = 10^7 ergs. Answer: 1 J = 10^7 ergs

Example 3: Dimensional Analysis

Question: Find the dimensional formula of force. Solution: From Newton's 2nd law: F = m x a. Dimensions of mass: [M]. Dimensions of acceleration: [L T^-2]. F = [M] x [L T^-2] = [M^1 L^1 T^-2]. Answer: [M^1 L^1 T^-2]

Example 4: Significant Figures in Calculations

Question: The length and breadth of a rectangle are 5.12 m and 2.0 m. Find the area with proper significant figures. Solution: Area = l x b = 5.12 x 2.0 = 10.24. 5.12 has 3 sig figs, 2.0 has 2 sig figs. For multiplication, result has same number of significant figures as the term with the least (2). Answer: 10.2 m^2

Example 5: Error Calculation

Question: If the percentage error in measuring the radius of a circle is 2%, find the percentage error in the area. Solution: Area of circle: A = pi r^2. % error in A = 2 x (% error in r) [power formula] = 2 x 2% = 4%. Answer: 4%

Example 6: Percentage Error in Product

Question: The mass of an object is measured with 2% error and its velocity with 3% error. Find the percentage error in kinetic energy. Solution: KE = 1/2 mv^2. % error in KE = % error in m + 2 x (% error in v) = 2% + 2 x 3% = 2% + 6% = 8%. Answer: 8%

Example 7: Error in Quotient

Question: The resistance R is given by R = V/I. If V is measured as 10.0 V +/- 0.2 V and I as 2.0 A +/- 0.1 A, find the percentage error in R. Solution: % error in V = 0.2/10.0 x 100 = 2%. % error in I = 0.1/2.0 x 100 = 5%. % error in R = % error in V + % error in I (quotient rule) = 2% + 5% = 7%. Answer: 7%

Example 8: Dimensional Consistency Check

Question: Show whether the equation v = u + at is dimensionally correct. Solution: LHS: v has dimensions [L T^-1]. RHS: u + at = [L T^-1] + [L T^-2][T] = [L T^-1] + [L T^-1]. Both sides have same dimensions [L T^-1]. Answer: Dimensionally correct (LHS = RHS)

Example 9: Significant Figures in Sum

Question: 2.3 + 4.56 = ? Solution: 2.3 has 1 decimal place, 4.56 has 2 decimal places. For addition, result should have same number of decimal places as the least precise term. 2.3 + 4.56 = 6.86 -> round to 1 decimal place = 6.9. Answer: 6.9

Example 10: Density with Unit Conversion

Question: Convert 500 g/cm^3 to kg/m^3. Solution: 500 g/cm^3 = 500 x (1/1000 kg) / (1/100 m)^3 = 500 x 0.001 kg / 0.000001 m^3 = 500 x 10^3 kg/m^3 = 500,000 kg/m^3. Answer: 500,000 kg/m^3 or 5 x 10^5 kg/m^3

PYQs

Previous Year Questions (PYQs) - Physical Quantities

Typical PYQ Types

Common PYQ Patterns

Summary

Summary - Physical Quantities

Key Takeaways

  • Physical quantities are measurable properties of nature; they form the basis of all physics.
  • There are 7 base quantities (mass, length, time, temperature, current, amount of substance, luminous intensity) and many derived quantities.
  • Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have both magnitude and direction.
  • Significant figures indicate the precision of a measurement; follow rules for arithmetic operations.
  • Errors are unavoidable; quantify them using absolute, relative, and percentage errors.
  • Dimensional analysis is a powerful tool for checking equations, deriving relations, and converting units.
  • The SI system (International System) provides a global standard for scientific communication.
  • There are prefixes from nano (10^-9) to giga (10^9) for convenience in expressing large/small quantities.

Important Formulas

  • Density: rho = m / V
  • Speed: v = d / t
  • Velocity: v = displacement / time
  • Acceleration: a = change in velocity / time
  • Force: F = m x a
  • Work: W = F x d
  • Power: P = W / t
  • Pressure: P = F / A
  • Density: rho = m / V

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Confusing scalar with vector quantities
  • Ignoring significant figures in final answers
  • Forgetting to convert units before calculation
  • Reporting more significant figures than the measurement justifies
  • Not checking dimensional consistency of equations

  5. If error in radius is 3%, error in volume of sphere is?

  7. What is the principle of homogeneity of dimensions?

Overview

Vectors - Physics

Overview

Vectors are quantities that have both magnitude and direction. They are essential for describing motion, force, and many other physical phenomena.

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the definition and representation of vectors
  • Learn vector operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication
  • Apply vectors to solve problems in mechanics
  • Understand unit vectors and vector components

Concepts

Key Concepts with Applications - Vectors

1. Vector Representation

  • Concept: Vectors represent quantities with magnitude and direction
  • Application: Velocity in navigation, force in engineering, displacement in pathology

2. Vector Addition (Parallelogram/Triangle Law)

  • Concept: Resultant vector from sum of two or more vectors
  • Application: Net force on an object, relative velocity, equilibrium of forces

3. Scalar (Dot) Product

  • Concept: A.B = |A||B|cos(theta), result is scalar
  • Application: Work done W = F.s, electric flux, projection of vector

4. Vector (Cross) Product

  • Concept: A x B = |A||B|sin(theta) n, result is a vector
  • Application: Torque tau = r x F, Angular momentum L = r x p, Magnetic force

5. Unit Vectors (i, j, k)

  • Concept: Vectors of magnitude 1 along coordinate axes
  • Application: Expressing vectors in component form, 3D geometry problems

6. Components of Vectors

  • Concept: Resolving a vector into perpendicular components
  • Application: Inclined plane problems, projectile motion analysis

7. Collinearity and Coplanarity

  • Concept: Conditions for vectors to be collinear (parallel) or coplanar
  • Application: Checking if points are collinear/coplanar, checking if vectors lie in same plane

8. Direction Cosines

  • Concept: Cosines of angles between vector and coordinate axes
  • Application: Finding direction of a line in 3D, direction of forces

9. Scalar Triple Product

  • Concept: [A B C] = A.(BxC), volume of parallelepiped
  • Application: Checking coplanarity of vectors, finding volume in geometry

10. Vector Triple Product

  • Concept: A x (B x C) = B(A.C) - C(A.B)
  • Application: Mechanics problems, simplifying vector expressions

Main Points

Main Points - Vectors

All Main Points (Bullet Points)

Introduction to Vectors

  • Vector has both magnitude and direction
  • Written as vec(A), A, or |A|
  • Magnitude is a positive scalar
  • Direction is the orientation of the vector

Types of Vectors

  • Zero vector: magnitude zero, no direction
  • Unit vector: magnitude 1, direction same as original (A-hat = A/|A|)
  • Equal vectors: same magnitude and direction
  • Collinear vectors: parallel to same line
  • Parallel vectors: same direction (angle 0)
  • Anti-parallel vectors: opposite direction (angle 180)
  • Coplanar vectors: lie in same plane
  • Position vector: from origin to a point
  • Displacement vector: from initial to final point

Vector Addition Laws

  • Triangle Law: third side gives resultant
  • Parallelogram Law: diagonal gives resultant
  • Polygon Law: for more than two vectors
  • R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta)
  • tan phi = (B sin theta)/(A + B cos theta)

Vector Subtraction

  • A - B = A + (-B)
  • R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 - 2AB cos theta)

Scalar (Dot) Product

  • A.B = |A||B|cos(theta)
  • A.B = A_x B_x + A_y B_y + A_z B_z
  • A.A = |A|^2
  • Commutative: A.B = B.A
  • Result is always a scalar

Vector (Cross) Product

  • A x B = |A||B|sin(theta) n
  • A x B = (A_y B_z - A_z B_y)i + (A_z B_x - A_x B_z)j + (A_x B_y - A_y B_x)k
  • A x B = -B x A (not commutative)
  • Result is a vector perpendicular to the plane

Unit Vectors (i, j, k)

  • i, j, k are unit vectors along x, y, z axes
  • A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k

Components

  • A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k
  • |A| = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2)
  • Direction cosines: cos alpha = A_x/|A|, cos beta = A_y/|A|, cos gamma = A_z/|A|
  • cos^2 alpha + cos^2 beta + cos^2 gamma = 1

Scalar Triple Product

  • [A B C] = A.(B x C)
  • Cyclic: [A B C] = [B C A] = [C A B]
  • Anti-cyclic: [A B C] = -[B A C]
  • [A B C] = 0 means vectors are coplanar

Vector Triple Product

  • A x (B x C) = B(A.C) - C(A.B)
  • Not associative

Applications

  • Work done: W = F.s (dot product)
  • Torque: tau = r x F (cross product)
  • Power: P = F.v (dot product)
  • Angular momentum: L = r x p (cross product)

Level 1 Key Points (Foundation)

  • Types of vectors (zero, unit, equal, collinear)
  • Vector addition laws (triangle, parallelogram)
  • Dot and cross product definition and properties
  • Unit vectors and component form
  • Magnitude and direction cosine formulas

  • Scalar triple product and coplanarity
  • Vector triple product
  • Application of dot product (work, projection)
  • Application of cross product (torque, angular momentum)
  • 3D vector problems and vector calculus basics

Level 1

Level 1 Topics - Vectors

Introduction to Vectors

  • Vector: A physical quantity with magnitude and direction (e.g., velocity, force, displacement)
  • Notation: Alphabet with arrow on top (vec{A}) or bold letters (A) or with line on both sides (|A|)
  • Magnitude: Length of the vector, always a positive scalar
  • Direction: The orientation of the vector in space

Representation of Vectors

  • Graphical method: Arrow with direction and proportional length
  • Component form: A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k (unit vectors form)
  • Polar form: A = A (cos theta i + sin theta j)

Types of Vectors

  • Zero vector: Magnitude zero, no direction (0)
  • Unit vector: Magnitude 1, direction same as original vector (A-hat = A/|A|)
  • Equal vectors: Same magnitude and direction
  • Collinear vectors: Parallel to the same line
  • Parallel vectors: Same direction (angle 0)
  • Anti-parallel vectors: Opposite direction (angle 180)
  • Coplanar vectors: Lie in the same plane
  • Position vector: From origin to a point in space

Vector Operations

  • Addition: Triangle law, Parallelogram law, Polygon law
  • Subtraction: A - B = A + (-B)
  • Scalar multiplication: How much vector stretches

Fundamental Definitions

  • Position vector: Vector from origin to the point
  • Displacement vector: From initial point to final point
  • Velocity vector: Time rate of change of displacement
  • Acceleration vector: Time rate of change of velocity

Level 2

Level 2 Topics - Vectors

Vector Addition Laws

  • Triangle Law: If two vectors act at a point, the third side of the triangle gives the resultant
  • Parallelogram Law: If two vectors act at a point, the diagonal of parallelogram gives the resultant
  • Polygon Law: For more than two vectors, close the polygon to get resultant

Magnitude of Resultant

  • R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta)
  • For A and B at right angles (theta = 90): R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2)
  • For equal vectors (A = B): R = 2A cos(theta/2)

Direction of Resultant

  • tan phi = (B sin theta) / (A + B cos theta)
  • phi = tan^-1((B sin theta) / (A + B cos theta))

Vector Subtraction

  • A - B = A + (-B) where -B is B with reversed direction
  • R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 - 2AB cos theta) when finding A - B

Scalar (Dot) Product

  • A . B = |A| |B| cos theta
  • Properties: commutative (A.B = B.A), distributive, A.A = |A|^2
  • Result is always a scalar

Vector (Cross) Product

  • A x B = |A| |B| sin theta n (n = unit vector perpendicular to plane)
  • Properties: non-commutative (A x B = -B x A), distributive
  • Result is always a vector perpendicular to the plane of A and B

Unit Vectors

  • Unit vector in direction of A: A-hat = A/|A|
  • i, j, k are unit vectors along x, y, z axes
  • Magnitude of unit vector = 1

Vector Components

  • A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k
  • A_x = A cos alpha, A_y = A cos beta, A_z = A cos gamma (direction cosines)
  • A = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2)

Scalar Triple Product

  • [A B C] = A . (B x C)
  • Represents volume of parallelepiped
  • Cyclic order: [A B C] = [B C A] = [C A B]
  • Anti-cyclic: [A B C] = -[B A C]

Vector Triple Product

  • A x (B x C) = B(A.C) - C(A.B)
  • Shows it is NOT associative

Resolution of Vectors

  • In 2D: A_x = A cos theta, A_y = A sin theta
  • In 3D: A_x = A sin theta cos phi, A_y = A sin theta sin phi, A_z = A cos theta
  • Resultant: A = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2)

Important Properties

  • Collinearity: Two non-zero vectors are collinear if A = k B (k is scalar)
  • Coplanarity: Three vectors are coplanar if [A B C] = 0
  • Orthogonal vectors: A and B are orthogonal if A.B = 0
  • Perpendicular vectors: A and B are perpendicular if A x B = 0 (for parallel condition) OR A . B = 0 (for perpendicular)

Examples

Examples - Vectors

Solved Examples

Example 1: Magnitude of Vector

Question: Find the magnitude of vector A = 3i + 4j. Solution: |A| = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5 Answer: |A| = 5

Example 2: Unit Vector

Question: Find the unit vector in the direction of A = 5i - 12j. Solution: |A| = sqrt(5^2 + (-12)^2) = sqrt(25 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13 A-hat = A/|A| = (5/13)i - (12/13)j Answer: A-hat = (5/13)i - (12/13)j

Example 3: Resultant of Two Vectors

Question: Find the magnitude of the resultant of A = 3i + 4j and B = 5i - 12j. Solution: A = 5, B = 13 (magnitudes). Angle between them: cos(theta) = (35 + 4(-12))/(5*13) = (15-48)/65 = -33/65 R = sqrt(5^2 + 13^2 + 2513(-33/65)) = sqrt(25 + 169 - 66) = sqrt(128) = 8sqrt(2) Answer: R = 8*sqrt(2)

Example 4: Scalar (Dot) Product

Question: Find the dot product of A = i + 2j and B = 3i - j. Solution: A.B = 13 + 2(-1) = 3 - 2 = 1 Answer: A.B = 1

Example 5: Cross Product

Question: Find the cross product of A = i + j and B = 2i - j. Solution: A = (1, 1, 0), B = (2, -1, 0) A x B = (1(-1) - 0(-1))k = -1k - 0k = -3k? Let me recalculate. A x B = (1(-1) - 12)k = (-1 - 2)k = -3k Answer: A x B = -3k

Example 6: Angle Between Vectors

Question: Find the angle between vectors A = i + j and B = i - j. Solution: A.B = 11 + 1(-1) = 0. Since A.B = 0, the vectors are perpendicular, so theta = 90 degrees. Answer: 90 degrees

Example 7: Work Done

Question: A force F = 3i + 4j N acts on a particle, displacement s = 2i + j m. Find work done. Solution: W = F.s = 32 + 41 = 6 + 4 = 10 J Answer: 10 J

Example 8: Torque (Cross Product)

Question: A force F = 2i + 3j acts at a point with position vector r = 4i. Find torque. Solution: tau = r x F = (4i) x (2i + 3j) = 43(i x j) = 12k Answer: tau = 12k (N m)

Example 9: Component of a Vector

Question: Find the component of A = 6i + 8j along the direction of B = 3i + 4j. Solution: |B| = sqrt(3^2 + 4^2) = 5. Component = A.B/|B| = (63 + 84)/5 = (18 + 32)/5 = 50/5 = 10 Answer: 10

Example 10: Scalar Triple Product

Question: Find the scalar triple product [A B C] where A = i + j, B = j + k, C = k + i. Solution: [A B C] = A.(B x C). B x C = i + j - k. A.(B x C) = (i + j).(i + j - k) = 1 + 1 + 0 = 2 Answer: 2

Summary

Summary - Vectors

Key Takeaways

  • Vectors have both magnitude and direction
  • Vectors are represented by arrow, bold letter, or with line (|A|)
  • Vector addition follows triangle, parallelogram, and polygon laws
  • Scalar (dot) product: A.B = |A||B|cos(theta), gives scalar
  • Vector (cross) product: A x B = |A||B|sin(theta)n, gives vector
  • Unit vectors: i, j, k for x, y, z axes
  • Components: A = A_x i + A_y j + A_z k
  • Resultant: R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta)
  • Angle between vectors: theta = cos^-1(A.B / |A||B|)
  • Direction cosines: cos alpha = A_x/|A|, cos beta = A_y/|A|, cos gamma = A_z/|A|
  • Zero vector: magnitude zero, no direction
  • Unit vector: magnitude 1, direction same as original
  • Collinear vectors: parallel to same line
  • Coplanar vectors: lie in same plane
  • Scalar triple product: [A B C] = A.(BxC), volume of parallelepiped
  • Vector triple product: A x (B x C) = B(A.C) - C(A.B)

Important Formulas

  • Resultant of two vectors: R = sqrt(A^2 + B^2 + 2AB cos theta)
  • Dot product: A.B = |A||B|cos(theta)
  • Cross product: A x B = |A||B|sin(theta) n (n = unit vector perpendicular to plane)
  • Angle between vectors: theta = cos^-1(A.B / |A||B|)
  • Magnitude of vector: |A| = sqrt(A_x^2 + A_y^2 + A_z^2)
  • Unit vector: A-hat = A/|A|
  • Direction cosines: cos alpha = A_x/|A|, cos beta = A_y/|A|, cos gamma = A_z/|A|
  • Work done: W = F.s (dot product)
  • Torque: tau = r x F (cross product)
  • Scalar triple product: [A B C] = A.(BxC)
  • Vector triple product: A x (B x C) = B(A.C) - C(A.B)

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Confusing dot product (scalar) with cross product (vector)
  • Ignoring direction when finding angle between vectors
  • Mixing up scalar and vector triple products
  • Not using right-hand rule for cross product direction
  • Forgetting that cross product is not commutative
  • Confusing collinearity with coplanarity

Overview

Lens - Physics

Overview

This topic covers refraction through lenses, image formation, lens formula, magnification, and power of a lens.

Learning Objectives

  • Understand refraction through lenses (convex and concave)
  • Learn about lens formula
  • Understand power of a lens
  • Apply lens maker's formula

Concepts

Key Concepts with Applications - Lens

1. Lens

  • Concept: Transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces
  • Application: Eyeglasses, cameras, microscopes, telescopes

2. Convex (Converging) Lens

  • Concept: Thicker at center, converges light
  • Application: Magnifying glass, camera lenses, human eye

3. Concave (Diverging) Lens

  • Concept: Thinner at center, diverges light
  • Application: Nearsightedness correction, peepholes

4. Lens Formula

  • Concept: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u
  • Application: Image position, focal length, object distance calculations

5. Magnification

  • Concept: m = h2/h1 = v/u
  • Application: Determining image size, nature

6. Power of Lens

  • Concept: P = 1/f (diopters)
  • Application: Prescribing corrective lenses (optical power)

7. Lens Maker's Formula

  • Concept: 1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)
  • Application: Designing lenses with specific focal lengths

8. Combination of Lenses

  • Concept: P_total = P1 + P2
  • Application: Telephoto lenses, microscopes, telescopes

9. Defects of Lenses

  • Concept: Spherical aberration (peripheral rays focus closer)
  • Application: Corrected with sophisticated lens designs

10. Applications Summary

  • Eyeglasses (correcting vision)
  • Camera lenses (focusing light)
  • Microscopes (magnification)
  • Telescopes (viewing distant objects)
  • Human eye (natural lens)
  • Projectors (image formation)

11. Numerical Problems

  • Find image position using lens formula
  • Find magnification
  • Find focal length of combination
  • Find power of lens
  • Lens maker's formula problems
  • Defect analysis

Main Points

Key Points - Lens

All Main Points (Bullet Points)

Lens Types

  • Convex (converging) lens: thicker at center, converges light rays
  • Concave (diverging) lens: thinner at center, diverges light rays
  • Types: biconvex, plano-convex, concavo-convex, biconcave, plano-concave, concavo-concave

Key Terms

  • Optical center (O): point where light passes undeviated
  • Principal axis: line through optical center and centers of curvature
  • Focus (F): converging point (convex) or apparent divergence point (concave)
  • Focal length (f): distance from optical center to focus
  • Power of lens (P): P = 1/f (diopters, D)

Image Formation by Convex Lens

  • At infinity: image at F (real, inverted, highly diminished)
  • Beyond 2F: between F and 2F (real, inverted, diminished)
  • At 2F: at 2F (real, inverted, same size)
  • Between F and 2F: beyond 2F (real, inverted, magnified)
  • At F: at infinity (real, inverted, highly magnified)
  • Between F and O: same side (virtual, erect, magnified)

Image Formation by Concave Lens

  • At infinity: at F (virtual, erect, highly diminished)
  • At finite distance: between F and O (virtual, erect, diminished)

Lens Formula

  • 1/f = 1/v - 1/u (Cartesian sign convention)
  • u = -ve (always, object on left)
  • f > 0 for convex, f < 0 for concave
  • v > 0: real image, v < 0: virtual image

Magnification

  • m = h2/h1 = v/u
  • m > 0: erect image, m < 0: inverted image
  • |m| > 1: magnified, |m| < 1: diminished

Power of Lens

  • P = 1/f (f in meters)
  • SI unit: diopters (D)
  • Convex: positive power, Concave: negative power
  • Combination: P = P1 + P2 (for lenses in contact)

Lens Maker's Formula

  • 1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)
  • n = refractive index of lens material
  • R1 = radius of curvature of first surface
  • R2 = radius of curvature of second surface

Defects of Lenses

  • Spherical aberration: peripheral rays focus nearer
  • Chromatic aberration: different colors focus at different points
  • Coma: off-axis point images distorted
  • Astigmatism: different focal lengths in different meridians
  • Presbyopia: aging eye, loss of accommodation

Applications

  • Eyeglasses: correcting vision (convex for farsightedness, concave for nearsightedness)
  • Camera lenses: focusing light
  • Microscopes: compound lenses for high magnification
  • Telescopes: objective and eyepiece lenses
  • Human eye: natural convex lens for focusing
  • Projectors: image projection

Level 1

Lens - Level 1

Lens

  • Lens: Transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces
  • Convex (converging) lens: Thicker at center, converges light rays
  • Concave (diverging) lens: Thinner at center, diverges light rays

Important Terms

  • Optical center (O): Point through which light passes undeviated
  • Principal axis: Line passing through optical center and centers of curvature
  • Focus (F): Point where parallel rays converge (convex) or appear to diverge (concave)
  • Focal length (f): Distance from optical center to focus
  • Power of lens (P): P = 1/f (in meters), measured in diopters (D)

Image Formation by Convex Lens

  • Object at infinity: Image at focus (real, inverted, highly diminished)
  • Object beyond 2F: Image between F and 2F (real, inverted, diminished)
  • Object at 2F: Image at 2F (real, inverted, same size)
  • Object between F and 2F: Image beyond 2F (real, inverted, enlarged)
  • Object at F: Image at infinity (real, inverted, highly enlarged)
  • Object between F and O: Image on same side (virtual, erect, enlarged)

Image Formation by Concave Lens

  • Object at infinity: Image at focus (virtual, erect, highly diminished)
  • Object at finite distance: Image between F and O (virtual, erect, diminished)

Lens Formula

  • 1/f = 1/v - 1/u (sign convention: u = object distance, v = image distance, f = focal length)

Magnification

  • m = h2/h1 = v/u (positive = erect image, negative = inverted image)

Level 2

Lens - Level 2

Lens Formula

  • 1/f = 1/v - 1/u (sign convention: u = object distance = always negative, v = image distance, f = focal length)
  • f > 0 for convex lens
  • f < 0 for concave lens

Sign Conventions (Cartesian)

  • All distances measured from optical center
  • Distances in direction of incident light = positive
  • Distances opposite to incident light = negative
  • Heights above principal axis = positive
  • Heights below principal axis = negative

Magnification

  • m = h2/h1 = v/u
  • m > 0: erect image, m < 0: inverted image
  • m > 1: magnified, m < 1: diminished

Power of Lens

  • P = 1/f (f in meters)
  • SI unit: diopters (D)
  • Convex lens: positive power, Concave lens: negative power
  • Combination of lenses: P = P1 + P2 + P3 (power adds)

Lens Maker's Formula

  • 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)
  • n = refractive index of lens material
  • R1 = radius of curvature of first surface
  • R2 = radius of curvature of second surface
  • R1 positive for convex, negative for concave

Combination of Lenses

  • 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2 (for two lenses separated by distance d)
  • When lenses are in contact: 1/F = 1/f1 + 1/f2
  • Power: P = P1 + P2

Defects of Lenses

  • Spherical aberration: Peripheral rays focus nearer than paraxial rays
  • Chromatic aberration: Different colors focus at different points
  • Coma: Off-axis point images distorted
  • Astigmatism: Different focal lengths in different meridians
  • Presbyopia: Aging eye, loss of accommodation

  2. Find magnification
  3. Find focal length of combination
  4. Find power of lens
  5. Lens maker's formula problems
  6. Defect analysis

InfinityAt FHighly diminished
Beyond 2FBetween F and 2FDiminished
At 2FAt 2FSame size
Between F and 2FBeyond 2FMagnified
At FAt infinityHighly magnified
Between F and OSame sideMagnified

Pitfalls

  • u is always negative
  • f positive for convex, negative for concave
  • v positive for real, negative for virtual
  • Power: P = 1/f with f in meters
  • Combination: P_total = P1 + P2

Examples

Examples - Lens

Solved Examples

Example 1: Lens Formula

Question: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. Find image position and nature. Solution: u = -20 cm (object distance), f = +15 cm (convex lens). 1/f = 1/v - 1/u 1/15 = 1/v - 1/(-20) 1/15 = 1/v + 1/20 1/v = 1/15 - 1/20 = 4/60 - 3/60 = 1/60 v = 60 cm Answer: v = 60 cm, real and inverted image (behind the lens)

Example 2: Magnification

Question: An object 5 cm tall is placed 30 cm from a convex lens (f = 20 cm). Find the size of the image. Solution: u = -30 cm, f = 20 cm. 1/20 = 1/v - 1/(-30) 1/20 = 1/v + 1/30 1/v = 1/20 - 1/30 = 3/60 - 2/60 = 1/60 v = 60 cm m = v/u = 60/(-30) = -2 h2 = m h1 = -2 5 = -10 cm (upside down and 2x larger) Answer: 10 cm, inverted

Example 3: Concave Lens

Question: An object is placed 30 cm from a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. Find image position. Solution: u = -30 cm, f = -15 cm (concave). 1/(-15) = 1/v - 1/(-30) -1/15 = 1/v + 1/30 1/v = -1/15 - 1/30 = -2/30 - 1/30 = -3/30 v = -10 cm Answer: v = -10 cm, virtual and erect

Example 4: Power of Lens

Question: Find the power of a convex lens of focal length 25 cm. Solution: P = 1/f (m) = 1/0.25 = 4 D Answer: 4 diopters (D)

Example 5: Lens Combination

Question: Two lenses of focal lengths 20 cm and 30 cm are placed in contact. Find the power of the combination. Solution: P = P1 + P2 = 1/0.2 + 1/0.3 = 5 + 3.33 = 8.33 D Answer: 8.33 D

Practice Exercise

  1. Convex lens, f = 15 cm, u = -30 cm, find v
  2. Concave lens, f = -10 cm, u = -20 cm, find v
  3. Lens power = 2 D, find focal length
  4. Two lenses: f1 = 10 cm, f2 = 20 cm, in contact, find combined power
  5. Object 4 cm tall, u = -20 cm, v = 30 cm, find magnification

Summary

Summary - Lens

Key Takeaways

  • Lens: transparent medium bounded by two spherical surfaces
  • Convex (converging) lens: thicker at center, converges light
  • Concave (diverging) lens: thinner at center, diverges light
  • Lens formula: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u (Cartesian sign convention)
  • Power of lens: P = 1/f (diopters, D)
  • Convex lens: positive power, concave: negative power
  • Power of combination: P = P1 + P2 (lenses in contact)
  • Magnification: m = h2/h1 = v/u (positive = erect, negative = inverted)
  • Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)
  • Defects: spherical aberration (peripheral rays), chromatic aberration (colors)
  • Applications: eyeglasses, cameras, microscopes, telescopes, human eye
  • Combination of lenses for magnifications and powers

Important Formulas

FormulaDescription
1/f = 1/v - 1/uLens formula
P = 1/fPower of lens (diopters)
P = P1 + P2Combination of lenses
m = h2/h1 = v/uMagnification
1/f = (n-1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)Lens maker's formula

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Sign conventions: f positive for convex, negative for concave
  • u is always negative (object on left side)
  • v positive: real image, v negative: virtual image
  • Not converting power to focal length (f = 1/P)
  • Mixing up convex (converging) with concave (diverging)

Overview

Reflection at Curved Mirror - Physics

Overview

This topic covers the reflection of light by curved mirrors (concave and convex), image formation, mirror formula, and magnification.

Learning Objectives

  • Understand reflection at spherical mirrors
  • Learn about concave and convex mirrors
  • Apply mirror formula and magnification
  • Understand sign conventions

Concepts

Key Concepts with Applications - Reflection at Curved Mirror

1. Reflection

  • Concept: Light bounces off a surface
  • Application: Shaving mirrors, makeup mirrors, reflectors

2. Concave Mirrors

  • Concept: Converging mirrors, focus real
  • Application: Dentist mirrors, solar cookers, headlights

3. Convex Mirrors

  • Concept: Diverging mirrors, focus virtual
  • Application: Rear-view mirrors, security mirrors, safety mirrors

4. Image Formation

  • Concept: Real or virtual, inverted or erect, magnified or diminished
  • Application: Understanding how mirrors form images

5. Mirror Formula

  • Concept: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
  • Application: Finding image position, focal length, object distance

6. Magnification

  • Concept: m = -v/u
  • Application: Determining image size, nature

7. Sign Conventions

  • Concept: Cartesian sign convention for mirrors
  • Application: Solving numerical problems systematically

8. Spherical Aberration

  • Concept: Different rays focus at different points
  • Application: Corrected with parabolic mirrors in telescopes

9. Uses Summary

  • Shaving/makeup mirrors (concave)
  • Dentist mirrors (concave, magnified)
  • Car headlights (concave with bulb at focus)
  • Rear-view mirrors (convex, wide field)
  • Security mirrors (convex, surveillance)
  • Solar furnaces (large concave mirrors)

10. Numerical Problems

  • Find focal length
  • Find image position
  • Find magnification
  • Find radius of curvature
  • Solve mirror equation problems

Main Points

Key Points - Reflection at Curved Mirror

All Main Points (Bullet Points)

Mirror Basics

  • Spherical mirror: part of hollow sphere
  • Concave: inner surface reflecting, converging
  • Convex: outer surface reflecting, diverging
  • Pole (P): center of mirror surface
  • Center of curvature (C): center of sphere
  • Radius of curvature (R): distance P to C
  • Principal axis: line through P and C
  • Focus (F): converging point (concave) or apparent divergence point (convex)
  • Focal length (f): distance P to F
  • f = R/2

Reflection

  • Law: angle of incidence = angle of reflection
  • Incident ray, reflected ray, normal in same plane

Sign Conventions (Cartesian)

  • All distances from pole
  • Distances in direction of incident light = positive
  • Distances opposite to incident light = negative
  • Heights above principal axis = positive
  • Heights below principal axis = negative
  • u = -ve (always, object in front)
  • f = -ve (concave), f = +ve (convex)
  • v = -ve: real image (in front)
  • v = +ve: virtual image (behind mirror)

Image Formation by Concave Mirror

  • At infinity: image at F (real, inverted, highly diminished)
  • Beyond C: between F and C (real, inverted, diminished)
  • At C: at C (real, inverted, same size)
  • Between C and F: beyond C (real, inverted, magnified)
  • At F: at infinity (real, inverted, highly magnified)
  • Between F and P: behind mirror (virtual, erect, magnified)

Image Formation by Convex Mirror

  • At infinity: at F (virtual, erect, highly diminished)
  • At finite distance: between P and F (virtual, erect, diminished)

Magnification

  • m = h2/h1 (positive = erect, negative = inverted)
  • m = -v/u
  • |m| > 1: magnified, |m| = 1: same size, |m| < 1: diminished

Uses

  • Shaving/makeup mirrors (concave)
  • Dentist mirrors (concave)
  • Car headlights (concave with bulb at focus)
  • Rear-view mirrors (convex, wide field)
  • Security mirrors (convex)
  • Solar cookers/furnaces (concave)

Spherical Aberration

  • Peripheral rays focus nearer than paraxial rays
  • Corrected with parabolic mirrors

Level 1

Reflection at Curved Mirror - Level 1

Curved Mirrors

  • Spherical mirror: Part of a hollow sphere
  • Concave mirror: Reflecting surface is the inner (concave) side
  • Convex mirror: Reflecting surface is the outer (convex) side
  • Pole (P): Center of the mirror surface
  • Center of curvature (C): Center of the sphere
  • Radius of curvature (R): Distance from pole to center of curvature
  • Principal axis: Line passing through pole and center of curvature
  • Focus (F): Point where parallel rays converge (concave) or appear to diverge (convex)
  • Focal length (f): Distance from pole to focus

Light Reflection

  • Laws of reflection: (1) Angle of incidence = Angle of reflection (2) Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane
  • Regular reflection: From smooth surface, parallel rays remain parallel
  • Diffuse reflection: From rough surface, rays scatter in all directions
  • Real image: Can be formed on a screen (formed by concave mirrors)
  • Virtual image: Cannot be formed on a screen (formed by convex mirrors, plane mirrors)

Image Formation by Concave Mirror

  • Object at infinity: Image at focus (real, inverted, highly diminished)
  • Object beyond C: Image between F and C (real, inverted, diminished)
  • Object at C: Image at C (real, inverted, same size)
  • Object between C and F: Image beyond C (real, inverted, enlarged)
  • Object at F: Image at infinity (real, inverted, highly enlarged)
  • Object between F and P: Image behind mirror (virtual, erect, enlarged)

Image Formation by Convex Mirror

  • Object at infinity: Image at focus (virtual, erect, highly diminished)
  • Object at finite distance: Image between P and F (virtual, erect, diminished)

Level 2

Reflection at Curved Mirror - Level 2

Mirror Formula

  • 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (sign convention: f = focal length, v = image distance, u = object distance)
  • u is always negative (object in front of mirror)
  • f is negative for concave, positive for convex
  • v is negative for real image (in front), positive for virtual (behind)

Sign Conventions (Cartesian)

  • All distances measured from pole
  • Distances in direction of incident light = positive
  • Distances opposite to incident light = negative
  • Heights above principal axis = positive
  • Heights below principal axis = negative

Magnification

  • m = h2/h1 (height of image / height of object)
  • m = -v/u (using distances)
  • m > 1: magnified, m < 1: diminished, m = 1: same size
  • m > 0: erect image, m < 0: inverted image

Relation between f and R

  • f = R/2 (focal length is half the radius of curvature)

Spherical Aberration

  • White bright spot at paraxial focus (paraxial rays focus nearer than marginal rays)
  • Causes blurry image

Uses of Concave Mirrors

  • Shaving mirrors (enlarged image)
  • Reflectors in cars, torches
  • Solar cookers (convergence)
  • Dentist mirrors

Uses of Convex Mirrors

  • Rear-view mirrors (wide field of view)
  • Security mirrors in shops
  • Safety mirrors at blind corners

Numerical Problems

  1. Find focal length using mirror formula
  2. Find magnification and nature of image
  3. Find position of object/image
  4. Find radius of curvature
  5. Solving mirror equation problems

m = h2/h1Magnification by heights

Sign Convention (Cartesian)

u (object distance)Always negative

f (convex mirror)Positive

v (virtual image)Positive

Convex mirror: f = 10 cm, R =20 cm

Pitfalls

  • Always apply sign conventions carefully
  • Remember u is always negative
  • Real images have negative v, virtual have positive v

Examples

Examples - Reflection at Curved Mirror

Solved Examples

Example 1: Mirror Formula

Question: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the image position and nature. Solution: u = -30 cm, f = -15 cm (concave). 1/f = 1/v + 1/u 1/(-15) = 1/v + 1/(-30) -1/15 = 1/v - 1/30 1/v = -1/15 + 1/30 = -2/30 + 1/30 = -1/30 v = -30 cm Answer: v = -30 cm, real and inverted image (same size as object)

Example 2: Magnification

Question: A concave mirror forms an image 3 times magnified. If object is at 10 cm, find image position. Solution: m = -v/u = 3 (magnified, real). u = -10 cm -v/(-10) = 3 v = 30 cm (negative for real) v = -30 cm Answer: v = -30 cm (in front of mirror)

Example 3: Focal Length

Question: Radius of curvature of a concave mirror is 40 cm. Find focal length. Solution: f = R/2 = 40/2 = 20 cm Answer: f = 20 cm

Example 4: Convex Mirror

Question: An object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find image position. Solution: u = -20 cm, f = +10 cm (convex). 1/10 = 1/v + 1/(-20) 1/10 = 1/v - 1/20 1/v = 1/10 + 1/20 = 3/20 v = 20/3 = 6.67 cm Answer: v = +6.67 cm, virtual and erect, behind the mirror

Example 5: Radius of Curvature

Question: A concave mirror produces a real image of an object placed 20 cm from it at 40 cm. Find radius of curvature. Solution: u = -20 cm, v = -40 cm. 1/f = 1/v + 1/u = 1/(-40) + 1/(-20) = -1/40 - 1/20 = -3/40 f = -40/3 = -13.33 cm R = 2f = -26.67 cm Answer: R = 26.67 cm

Summary

Summary - Reflection at Curved Mirror

Key Takeaways

  • Mirror formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u
  • Focal length f = R/2 (R = radius of curvature)
  • Concave mirrors: converging, real focus
  • Convex mirrors: diverging, virtual focus
  • Sign convention: u = -ve (object in front), f = -ve (concave), f = +ve (convex)
  • v = -ve: real image (in front of mirror)
  • v = +ve: virtual image (behind mirror)
  • m = -v/u: +ve (erect), -ve (inverted), |m| > 1 (magnified), |m| < 1 (diminished)
  • Concave mirrors: shaving/makeup mirrors, headlights, solar cookers, dentist mirrors
  • Convex mirrors: rear-view mirrors, security mirrors, wide field of view
  • Conservation of light: angle of incidence = angle of reflection

Important Formulas

FormulaDescription
1/f = 1/v + 1/uMirror formula
f = R/2Focal length-radius relationship
m = h2/h1Magnification (heights)
m = -v/uMagnification (distances)
R = 2fRadius of curvature
i = rLaw of reflection

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Forgetting sign conventions
  • Confusing concave (f negative) with convex (f positive)
  • Not identifying real vs virtual images correctly
  • Rounding errors in calculations
  • Mistaking v sign for real/virtual images

Overview

Refraction at Plane Surfaces - Physics

Overview

This topic covers the refraction (bending) of light as it passes from one medium to another at a plane surface, including laws of refraction, refractive index, and apparent depth.

Learning Objectives

  • Understand the laws of refraction
  • Learn about refractive index
  • Apply Snell's law
  • Understand apparent depth and total internal reflection

Concepts

Key Concepts with Applications - Refraction at Plane Surfaces

1. Refraction of Light

  • Concept: Bending of light when it passes from one medium to another
  • Application: Fish appearing closer in water, bending of straw in a glass

2. Laws of Refraction

  • Concept: Snell's law governs refraction
  • Application: Lens design, corrective lenses, fiber optics

3. Refractive Index

  • Concept: n = c/v measures optical density
  • Application: Gemology (diamond n=2.42), lens design

4. Snell's Law

  • Concept: n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r)
  • Application: Calculating angles of refraction in lens systems

5. Apparent Depth

  • Concept: Objects appear closer when viewed through a medium
  • Application: Fishermen seeing fish at shallower depth, pool depth measurement

6. Total Internal Reflection

  • Concept: Light trapped inside denser medium
  • Application: Diamond brilliance, optical fibers, mirage, binoculars

7. Critical Angle

  • Concept: Angle of incidence for 90-degree refraction
  • Application: Fiber optics, diamond cutting, underwater vision

8. Lateral Shift

  • Concept: Perpendicular distance between incident and emergent rays
  • Application: Glass slab problems, optical instruments

Key Points - Refraction at Plane Surfaces

All Main Points (Bullet Points)

Refraction Basics

  • Refraction: bending of light when passing from one medium to another
  • Cause: change in speed of light between media
  • Denser medium: light slows down, bends toward normal
  • Rarer medium: light speeds up, bends away from normal

Laws of Refraction

  • First law: incident ray, refracted ray, normal lie in the same plane
  • Second law (Snell's law): n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r)

Refractive Index

  • Absolute: n = c/v (speed in vacuum ÷ speed in medium)
  • Relative: n21 = n2/n1 = v1/v2
  • n is always > 1 for real media (compared to vacuum)
  • Optical density: higher n = optically denser

Snell's Law

  • n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r)
  • Applications: lens design, calculating angles in optical systems

Apparent Depth

  • Formula: Apparent depth = Real depth / n
  • Objects appear closer when viewed from rarer medium
  • Applications: fishing (prey appears closer), swimming pools

Total Internal Reflection

  • Condition: n1 > n2 AND angle of incidence > critical angle
  • Critical angle: sin(C) = n2/n1
  • Applications: diamond brilliance, optical fibers, mirage

Lateral Shift

  • Perpendicular distance between incident and emergent rays
  • Formula: l = t * sin(i - r) / cos(r)
  • Depends on thickness, angle of incidence, refractive index

Level 1

Refraction at Plane Surfaces - Level 1

Refraction of Light

  • Refraction: Bending of light when it passes from one medium to another at an angle
  • Cause: Change in speed of light when moving between media
  • Denser medium: Light slows down (bends toward normal)
  • Rarer medium: Light speeds up (bends away from normal)

Laws of Refraction

  • First law: Incident ray, refracted ray, and normal all lie in the same plane
  • Second law (Snell's law): sin(i)/sin(r) = constant (refractive index)

Refractive Index

  • Absolute refractive index: n = c/v where c = speed in vacuum, v = speed in medium
  • Relative refractive index: n21 = v1/v2
  • Optical density: Higher refractive index = optically denser
  • Units: Refractive index has no units (ratio of speeds)

Apparent Depth

  • Apparent depth: When viewing an object submerged in a medium, it appears closer
  • Formula: Apparent depth = Real depth / n
  • Applications: Fishermen see fish closer than actual depth

Total Internal Reflection

  • Condition: Light travels from denser to rarer medium
  • Critical angle: Angle of incidence in denser medium for which angle of refraction = 90 degrees
  • Total internal reflection: When angle of incidence > critical angle, light is completely reflected back
  • Applications: Mirage, diamond brilliance, optical fibers

Level 2

Refraction at Plane Surfaces - Level 2

Refractive Index

  • Absolute refractive index: n = c/v
  • Relative refractive index: n21 = v1/v2 or n21 = n2/n1
  • Snell's law: n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r)
  • Laws: Incident ray, refracted ray, normal in same plane
  • Total internal reflection: Occurs when n1 > n2 and angle of incidence > critical angle

Critical Angle

  • Definition: Angle of incidence in denser medium for which angle of refraction = 90 degrees
  • Formula: sin(C) = n2/n1 (n1 > n2)
  • Applications: Diamond brilliance, optical fibers, mirage
  • Total internal reflection: When i > C, light is completely reflected back

Apparent Depth

  • Apparent depth = Real depth / n (when viewing from rarer medium)
  • **Real depth = Apparent depth * n** (when viewing from denser medium)
  • Factors: Depends on refractive index of medium

Lateral Shift

  • Definition: Perpendicular distance between incident ray and emergent ray
  • Formula: l = t * sin(i - r) / cos(r) (t = thickness of slab)
  • Normal shift: d = t * (1 - cos(i - r)) / cos(r)

Lens Maker's Formula (Advanced)

  • 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)
  • n = refractive index of lens material
  • R1, R2 = radii of curvature of lens surfaces
  • R1 positive for convex, negative for concave

Examples

Examples - Refraction at Plane Surfaces

Solved Examples

Example 1: Snell's Law

Question: Light passes from air (n=1) into water (n=1.33) at an angle of incidence of 30 degrees. Find angle of refraction. Solution: n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r) 1 sin(30) = 1.33 sin(r) 0.5 = 1.33 * sin(r) sin(r) = 0.5/1.33 = 0.3759 r = sin^(-1)(0.3759) = 22.1 degrees Answer: 22.1 degrees

Example 2: Apparent Depth

Question: A coin lies at the bottom of a water tank 2 m deep. What is the apparent depth (n_water = 1.33)? Solution: Apparent depth = Real depth / n = 2/1.33 = 1.5 m Answer: 1.5 m

Example 3: Critical Angle

Question: Find the critical angle for light passing from water (n=1.33) to air (n=1). Solution: sin(C) = n_air/n_water = 1/1.33 = 0.7519 C = sin^(-1)(0.7519) = 48.8 degrees Answer: 48.8 degrees

Example 4: Total Internal Reflection

Question: Can light going from water (n=1.33) to air (n=1) at 50 degrees undergo total internal reflection? Solution: Critical angle = 48.8 degrees (from Example 3). Since i (50 degrees) > C (48.8 degrees), total internal reflection occurs. Answer: Yes, total internal reflection occurs

Example 5: Lateral Shift

Question: A light ray passes through a glass slab (n=1.5, thickness = 2 cm) at an angle of incidence of 45 degrees. Find lateral shift. Solution: r = sin^(-1)(sin(45)/1.5) = sin^(-1)(0.707/1.5) = sin^(-1)(0.4713) = 28.1 degrees l = t sin(i - r) / cos(r) = 2 sin(45 - 28.1) / cos(28.1) = 2 * sin(16.9) / cos(28.1) = 2 * 0.2905 / 0.882 = 0.658 cm Answer: 0.658 cm

Practice Exercise

  1. Refractive index of water 1.33, angle of incidence 45 degrees, find angle of refraction
  2. Apparent depth = 1.2 m, real depth = 1.5 m, find n
  3. Critical angle for diamond (n=2.42) to air
  4. Lateral shift through 3 cm slab at 30 degrees
  5. Light passing from glass (n=1.5) to water (n=1.33), angle of incidence 30 degrees

Summary

Summary - Refraction at Plane Surfaces

Key Takeaways

  • Laws of refraction: (1) Incident, refracted ray, and normal lie in the same plane (2) n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r)
  • Refractive index: n = c/v (speed in vacuum / speed in medium)
  • Light bends towards normal when entering denser medium, away from normal when entering rarer medium
  • Snells law: n1 sin(i) = n2 sin(r)
  • Apparent depth: Real depth / n
  • Total internal reflection: Occurs when light travels from denser to rarer medium, i > critical angle
  • Critical angle: sin(C) = n2/n1 (n1 > n2)
  • Applications: Diamonds (high n = brilliance), optical fibers (TIR for communication), mirage (TIR in hot air)
  • Lateral shift depends on: thickness, angle of incidence, refractive index
  • n is always > 1 for any medium (compared to vacuum)
  • Relative refractive index n21 = n2/n1

  • Forgetting total internal reflection only happens when light goes from denser to rarer
  • Not converting degrees to radians if required
  • Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal

Key Points - Refraction through Prism

All Main Points (Bullet Points)

Prism Basics

  • Prism: transparent medium bounded by three plane surfaces (triangular)
  • Angle of prism (A): angle between two refracting surfaces
  • Refracting surfaces: two surfaces through which light enters and emerges

Refraction through Prism

  • Incident ray: enters prism from air
  • Refracted ray: inside prism
  • Emergent ray: emerges from other face
  • Deviation (D): angle between incident ray and emergent ray
  • A + D = i + e (prism equation)

Minimum Deviation

  • Least deviation of light by prism
  • Condition: i = e, r1 = r2 = A/2
  • Prism formula: n = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2)

Dispersion of Light

  • Splitting of white light into constituent colors (VIBGYOR)
  • Cause: different colors have different n (n_blue > n_red)
  • Violet bends most, red least
  • Order: V, I, B, G, Y, O, R

Recombination

  • Second inverted prism recombines spectrum to white light
  • Demonstrates white light composition

Rainbow Formation

  • Primary rainbow: one internal reflection (red on top, violet on bottom)
  • Secondary rainbow: two internal reflections (violet on top, red on bottom)

Applications

  • Spectrometer: measures refractive indices
  • Binoculars: prisms erect image
  • Periscope: prisms for reflection
  • Diamond: brilliance through dispersion and TIR

Level 1

Refraction through Prism - Level 1

Prism

  • Prism: A transparent medium bounded by three plane surfaces
  • Triangular prism: Two triangular bases and three rectangular lateral surfaces
  • Angle of prism (A): Angle between the two refracting faces

Refraction through a Prism

  • Incident ray: Enters the prism from air
  • Refracted ray: Inside the prism
  • Emergent ray: Emerges from the other face
  • Angle of deviation (D): Angle between the incident ray extended and emergent ray
  • Minimum deviation (D_min): Lowest deviation when ray passes symmetrically

Prism Formula

  • A + D = i1 + i2 (at minimum deviation, D = D_min, i1 = i2)
  • For small angle prism: D ≈ (n - 1)A

Dispersion of Light

  • Dispersion: Splitting of white light into its constituent colors
  • Cause: Different colors have different refractive indices (violet bends most, red least)
  • Spectrum: VIBGYOR (Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red)
  • Newton's experiment: White light through prism produces spectrum, second prism recombines to white

Applications

  • Rainbow formation
  • Spectrometer for measuring refractive indices
  • Prism in binoculars, cameras
  • Weather balloons, periscopes

Level 2

Refraction through Prism - Level 2

Prism Formula

  • A + D = i1 + i2 (angle of prism + angle of deviation = sum of angles of incidence and emergence)
  • At minimum deviation: D = D_min, i1 = i2 = i, r1 = r2 = r
  • A = 2r (r = A/2 at minimum deviation)
  • i = (A + D_min)/2
  • n = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2) (refractive index from prism formula)

Deviation by Prism

  • Total deviation (D): Angle between incident ray and emergent ray
  • Conditions for minimum deviation: Prism in air, symmetric passage
  • Deviation depends on: Angle of prism, refractive index, angle of incidence
  • Dispersion: Different colors deviate differently (n_violet > n_red)

Dispersion of Light

  • VIBGYOR: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red
  • Order: Violet deviates most, Red least (n_violet > n_indigo > ... > n_red)
  • White light: Contains all colors; prism splits into spectrum
  • Recombination: Second inverted prism recombines spectrum to white light
  • Cause: n varies with wavelength (n_blue > n_red)

Rainbow Formation

  • Primary rainbow: One internal reflection in water droplets, colors: red on top, violet on bottom
  • Secondary rainbow: Two internal reflections, colors: violet on top, red on bottom

Applications

  • Spectrometer for measuring refractive indices
  • Prism in binoculars, cameras (erecting prism)
  • Periscopes
  • Diamond cutting for brilliance
  • Mirage formation (total internal reflection)

n_blue > n_green > n_redDispersion order
VIBGYORColor order (Violet to Red)

Prism Equation Breakdown

At minimum deviation:

  • A + D_min = 2i (since i = e)
  • A = 2r (since r1 = r2)
  • i = (A + D_min)/2
  • r = A/2
  • n = sin(i)/sin(r) = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2)

Examples

Examples - Refraction through Prism

Solved Examples

Example 1: Prism Formula

Question: The angle of prism is 60 degrees. The angle of minimum deviation is 30 degrees. Find the refractive index. Solution: n = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2) n = sin((60 + 30)/2) / sin(60/2) n = sin(45) / sin(30) = 0.707 / 0.5 = 1.414 Answer: n = 1.414

Example 2: Angle of Prism

Question: For a prism with n = 1.5, angle of minimum deviation is 30 degrees. Find angle of prism. Solution: n = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2) 1.5 = sin((A + 30)/2) / sin(A/2) 1.5 * sin(A/2) = sin((A + 30)/2) Using approximation for thin prisms: A ≈ D_min/(n-1) = 30/0.5 = 60 degrees Answer: A ≈ 60 degrees

Example 3: Deviation by Prism

Question: A ray of light passes through a prism of angle 50 degrees and emerges at an angle of emergence of 40 degrees. If the angle of incidence is 35 degrees, find angle of deviation. Solution: A + D = i + e 50 + D = 35 + 40 D = 75 - 50 = 25 degrees Answer: 25 degrees

Example 4: Dispersion of Light

Question: White light passes through a prism. Which color bends the most? Why? Solution: Violet bends the most because it has the shortest wavelength and highest refractive index (n_violet > n_red). Answer: Violet bends the most

Example 5: Rainbow

Question: Explain the formation of a primary rainbow. Solution: Sunlight enters water droplets, undergoes refraction, internal reflection (one reflection), and emerges with dispersion. Red is on top, violet on bottom. Answer: Formed by one internal reflection in water droplets

Practice Exercise

  1. Angle of prism = 60 degrees, angle of minimum deviation = 37 degrees, find n
  2. n = 1.5, angle of prism = 60 degrees, find D_min
  3. i = 40 degrees, e = 30 degrees, A = 50 degrees, find D
  4. Light through prism - which color deviates most? Which least?
  5. Primary rainbow - how many internal reflections?

Summary - Refraction through Prism

Key Takeaways

  • Prism: triangular glass block with two refracting surfaces
  • Angle of prism (A): Angle between two refracting surfaces
  • Angle of deviation (D): Angle between incident ray and emergent ray
  • Prism formula: n = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2)
  • At minimum deviation: A + D = i + e, r1 = r2 = A/2
  • Dispersion: Splitting of white light into VIBGYOR colors
  • Violet bends most, Red least (different wavelengths, different n)
  • Primary rainbow: One internal reflection (red on top)
  • Secondary rainbow: Two internal reflections (violet on top)
  • Applications: Spectrometer, binoculars, periscope, diamond cutting
  • Refractive index affects dispersion (n_blue > n_red)
  • Newton's experiment: First prism splits white light, second recombines to white

Important Formulas

FormulaDescription
A + D = i + ePrism equation
n = sin((A + D_min)/2) / sin(A/2)Prism formula
D ≈ (n - 1)AThin prism deviation
i = (A + D_min)/2At minimum deviation
A = 2rAt minimum deviation
VIBGYOROrder of colors

Common Mistakes to Avoid

  • Confusing angle of prism (A) with angle of deviation (D)
  • Forgetting that minimum deviation is the least possible deviation
  • Using wrong formula for dispersion
  • Not knowing that prism formula gives refractive index
  • Mixing up primary vs secondary rainbow

Applications

Applications of Refraction through Prism

Real-World Applications

  1. Spectrometer: Measures refractive indices of materials
  2. Binoculars: Prisms erect the image (compact design)
  3. Periscope: Uses prisms for reflection (no mirrors)
  4. Diamond Cutting: Dispersion and total internal reflection for brilliance
  5. Rainbow Formation: Natural prism effect in raindrops
  6. Spectroscopy: Analyzing light sources
  7. White Light: Understanding composition of white light
  8. Color Filter Design: Based on dispersion properties
  9. Weather Balloons: Atmospheric studies with spectrometers
  10. Laser Systems: Prisms used for beam steering

Industry Standards

  • Optical: Prism manufacturing standards
  • Scientific: Spectrometer precision
  • Aerospace: Prism-based systems
